questions.q: What is Derry’s physical condition and how did it happen, according to the text?
questions.a: Derry is a 14-year-old boy with one side of his face burned by acid ("I got acid all down that side of my face and it burned it all away. It ate my face up."). A wrong answer (e.g., "fire burn" or "birth defect") shows the student hasn’t read the specific cause — acid — which matters because acid implies sudden, violent damage, reinforcing Derry’s sense of violation and permanence.

questions.q: Why does Derry say, "People are afraid of me," and what does this reveal about his self-perception?
questions.a: Derry believes people recoil at his face ("You think... 'That’s bad. That’s a terrible thing... Poor boy.' But I’m not. Not poor. Underneath, you are afraid."). This reveals he has internalised others’ reactions: he sees himself *through their eyes* and equates his worth with his appearance. A wrong answer focusing only on "people stare" misses the psychological depth — Derry isn’t just observed; he *feels* their fear as a verdict on his humanity.

questions.q: Apply the concept of "masking" to Derry’s behaviour in Scene 1. How does he use anger and withdrawal to protect himself?
questions.a: Derry masks vulnerability with aggression: he snaps "I’m not afraid" then admits "People are afraid of me." He climbs the wall (not the open gate) to avoid interaction. When Mr Lamb offers friendship, Derry tests him: "Why don’t you ask me? ... You’re afraid to." This applies the psychological concept of defence mechanisms — Derry pushes people away before they can reject him. A wrong answer that calls him "just rude" misses the protective function of his hostility.

questions.q: Analyse the shift in Derry’s language from Scene 1 ("I’m not afraid" / "I don’t like being with people") to Scene 2 ("Things that matter. Things nobody else has ever said"). What does this linguistic change signal?
questions.a: Scene 1 language is defensive, absolute ("never", "nobody", "always"), and self-referential ("my face", "me"). Scene 2 language turns outward: "listen to things", "think about", "help him with the crab apples". The shift from *closed* to *open* vocabulary signals internal reorientation — he values *thinking* over *hiding*. A wrong answer that only quotes lines without comparing function misses the structural evidence of change.

questions.q: Evaluate whether Derry’s transformation by the end of Scene 3 is earned or implausible. Use three textual moments to justify your judgment.
questions.a: It is earned because: (1) Scene 1: Mr Lamb refuses pity ("Not the whole of you. Not of you") and models acceptance of his own disability ("Tin doesn’t hurt... It doesn’t signify"). (2) Scene 2: Derry *chooses* to return despite his mother’s prohibition ("If I don’t go back there, I’ll never go anywhere in this world again") — agency, not persuasion. (3) Scene 3: He runs back, finds Mr Lamb fallen, and weeps *but stays* ("I came back. Lamey-Lamb. I did... come back"). The arc moves from isolation → connection → loss → commitment. A wrong answer calling it "sudden" ignores the three-scene scaffolding.

questions.q: Create an alternative ending: Derry returns to the garden but Mr Lamb has died. Write Derry’s internal monologue (5–6 lines) showing whether he retreats or stays, using his voice from the play.
questions.a: A strong answer mirrors Derry’s vocabulary ("world", "listen", "choose", "risk") and shows agency: "The gate’s still open. He knew I’d come. / My legs work. The bees still hum. / I’ll pull the crab apples. I’ll make the jelly. / No curtains. Just light. / I choose this." A poor answer has Derry revert to "I’m ugly, I’ll hide" — contradicting Scene 2’s declaration that his face "isn’t important."

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Character analysis of the protagonist (Derry) in "On the Face of It" involves a systematic examination of his physical traits, psychological state, motivations, internal conflicts, speech patterns, relationships, and ______ across the play, using textual evidence to support inferences about his journey from alienation to tentative hope.
Fill in the blank: ______ you have a visible scar that makes strangers whisper.
Fill in the blank: Start by listing every line Derry speaks in Scene ______; notice how he interrupts Mr Lamb, assumes pity, and reveals his acid injury.
What must you be able to do to master this topic?
questions.a: The student can write a structured, evidence-based character analysis of Derry that traces his psychological arc across all three scenes, identifies the catalyst for his change, and explains how his dialogue and actions reveal a shift from self-loathing to agency, using the PEEL (Point, Evidence, Explanation, Link) paragraph structure.

questions.q: Fill in the blank: Imagine you have a visible scar that makes ______ whisper.
